You pass if you named three subsystems along those lines, one for reading, one for computing, one for producing output, and wrote one facade function that calls all three in that order without exposing the order to its caller. Naming only one subsystem that does all three jobs is a fail: that is a class with one job, not several subsystems for a facade to coordinate. Naming the three correctly but calling them from
instead of from one facade function is a partial pass.

Facade is a structural pattern that puts one simple entry point in front of several subsystems a caller would otherwise have to coordinate for itself. The subsystems it hides can be anything with its own interface and its own rules: a parser, a set of calculations, a hardware bus that has to start in a fixed order. The facade calls each of them in the right order and hides that order, and every one of the calls, behind a single function.

The problem is a sequence of calls that has to happen the same way everywhere it is needed, with the same checks and the same order, repeated at every call site that needs it. Bring up a robot's power, then its sensors, then its motion controller, and every place that starts the robot has to remember that order and handle a failure at each step, or copy code that already got it right somewhere else.

The mechanism is a class holding the subsystems, offering one function that does what all those call sites used to do by hand: call each subsystem, in order, stopping on the first failure. Nothing about the subsystems changes, and nothing about their interfaces is translated the way an adapter would; a facade calls several interfaces, it does not stand in for any one of them.

What it costs is that the subsystems stay reachable directly unless the facade goes out of its way to hide them, so a caller can still call one out of order and reproduce the exact bug the facade exists to prevent. It also grows past its purpose the moment every feature that touches any of its subsystems gets its own method on the facade, until the facade depends on the whole system and nothing depends on less than all of it.
You meet this the moment start-up, shutdown or a whole pipeline needs to be one call, and the interview question is exactly what a facade hides, and where that stops being enough.

Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides define Facade in the structural chapter of the 1994 catalogue (
) as an object that offers one interface to a set of interfaces in a subsystem, chosen for whatever a typical caller needs most of the time, not for completeness.
That is worth pausing on: a facade is not required to expose everything the subsystems can do, and it does not have to be the only way to reach them.

on its own, without starting anything, is not a case the facade has to serve. The pattern this creates is often confused with Adapter, which the previous topic covered, so it is worth stating the difference in one line: an adapter takes one adaptee and reshapes it to match one interface a caller already has, a one-to-one translation that changes nothing about what the adaptee computes; a facade takes several unrelated subsystems and offers one new interface that matches none of them individually, a many-to-one coordination that adds behaviour of its own, the order and the failure handling, that no single subsystem had.
A facade can hold an adapter as one of its subsystems, and often does: if
were a vendor SDK with its own vocabulary, the adapter topic's wrapper would sit between it and

would be none the wiser. The two patterns answer different questions, one interface reshaped to fit another, or several interfaces coordinated behind a new one, and a real system uses both at once far more often than it uses either alone.

Every one of those methods is reasonable on its own, and the class that results depends on every subsystem in the process, coordinating everything, doing everything, one method call away from a change in any part of the system. Brown, Malveau, Mowbray and McCormick catalogued this shape in 1998 as the Blob antipattern (

): one class that has taken on so much that everything else around it becomes a passive holder of data the Blob reaches into. The dependency injection topic's own heuristic still applies here without changing a word: a class that needs eight dependencies is a class doing eight things, and a facade is no more exempt from that count than any other class, only slower to notice, because each dependency arrived with a feature that looked like it belonged.

Facade and Adapter answer different questions, and confusing them produces the wrong fix in both directions. Reaching for a facade to solve an adapter's problem gives a coordinating class in front of one object, a wrapper that calls one thing and adds nothing. Reaching for an adapter to solve a facade's problem gives one class inheriting four unrelated interfaces at once, which still compiles, but the moment two of them declare a function with the same name, the two meanings collapse into whatever single override that class provides, or, left unoverridden, an unqualified call to that name is refused as ambiguous until every call site names which interface it means. The question worth asking before writing either is how many things are being wrapped, one adaptee reshaped to fit, or several subsystems coordinated into a sequence a caller should not have to write out by hand.
